title: Polly Klaas’s murder is routinely used to justify the death penalty. As her sisters, we oppose it | Annie Nichol and Jess Nichol
text:
For more than three decades, our sister Polly Klaas’s murder has been used to justify California’s death penalty.
When people debate the merit of punitive policies passed in Polly’s name, politicians, advocates, even strangers have asked: “What about Polly?” As if our loss were an argument that speaks for itself.
After so many years of hearing our family’s tragedy invoked in support of capital punishment, we wanted to make clear where we actually stand.
A few weeks ago, we met with the California governor, Gavin Newsom, on the former death row at San Quentin to explain why we do not support the death penalty. He has since said that conversation helped shape his decision to commute California’s death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
We wholeheartedly embrace that decision as a critical step toward a more just system.
We are writing to share what we have learned over more than 30 years of living alongside a system that promises justice, but has given California an expensive, error-prone process that prolongs trauma rather than preventing harm.
In our case, Polly’s killer was convicted and sentenced to death. More than 30 years later, he is still on death row.
If you’ve ever wondered what the death penalty “does” for victims’ families, that fact is a good place to start. A death sentence does not bring closure. It binds families to decades of hearings, legal filings, and headlines – keeping us tethered to the person who harmed us when what we want is to be able to move on with our lives and learn how to heal.
To be clear: we admire survivors who have done the courageous work of finding forgiveness for the people who harmed them or their loved ones. In our case, we have not forgiven the man who killed our sister. We still feel moments of intense grief and anger, as is natural after a loss like ours, and we still feel the persistent pain of Polly’s absence.
Even so, the feelings of vengeance so many survivors experience – however understandable – should not be the basis for public policy.
Survivors’ anger is real, and it deserves a response. The state can honor survivors’ anger without turning to an irreversible punishment. Yet while the death penalty is often justified in the name of victims, survivors’ needs are as varied as the harms we have lived through.
For many of us, the long arc of healing creates the space to ask deeper questions about what justice would actually require: what might help us recover, what could prevent another person from experiencing the same harm, and what forms of accountability might be possible.
Instead, the criminal legal system appropriates those questions and offers punishment as a one-size-fits-all substitute for the far more complicated work of healing, accountability and prevention.
Capital punishment exploits survivors’ most vulnerable moments of rage and pain. Our criminal legal system isn’t built to support the slow, human process of recovering from trauma – even though, for survivors, our grief changes shape over time, and the meaning we make of our loss changes with it.
Most survivors, however, are given no resources to help them heal or recover from their trauma.
In California, fewer than one in five survivors receive counseling, medical assistance or financial support after surviving a violent crime. This means many people remain in that pit of anger and trauma for their entire lives. They are told that punishment is the only justice they are allowed to ask for or expect, and far too often, the only “help” the system offers to survivors is the promise that someone else will suffer, too.
Survivors deserve more than this. They deserve healing, safety and counseling, the ability to pay for medical bills and housing and take care of their children – not an execution carried out decades later as a substitution for care.
Nonpartisan analysts have estimated that ending the death penalty in practice and converting death sentences to life without parole could save California taxpayers up to $150m annually, largely by reducing the extraordinary costs unique to capital cases. Imagine what $150m a year could mean if we invested it in the programs that actually prevent harm: mental health treatment, substance use intervention, gun violence prevention, trauma recovery centers, and support for survivors navigating the long aftermath of violence. Imagine what it will mean for solving cases, preventing future victimization, and stabilizing families before people fall through the cracks.
Nothing will undo our loss, and we don’t ask anyone to pretend otherwise. What we are asking is that California stop treating survivors’ pain as permission for state killing – and start choosing a public safety approach that supports healing and prevents harm.
To this day, people still invoke Polly’s name as if it settles the debate. It doesn’t. Execution isn’t a system responding to victims’ needs. It’s a system borrowing our pain to justify what it already intended to do.
We are grateful that Newsom has made these commutations a part of his legacy. Families like ours shouldn’t be trapped in an endless loop of promised violence. Instead, we should be building a public safety strategy that is bigger than vengeance – one that treats survivors as whole human beings, not as instruments of punishment.
We loved Polly. We miss her. We carry her with us. We deserve better than the death penalty. And so do all survivors.
- Annie and Jess Nichol are survivor advocates working to replace punitive responses to harm with healing, accountability and care
